author: Tertullian
occasion: Heretical teachers were using Scripture to draw Christians away from the faith, and Tertullian writes to show that heretics should not be allowed to appeal to Scripture at all, since the Scriptures belong to the apostolic churches.
argument: Heresies were predicted by Christ and the apostles, so their existence should not disturb believers; they serve to test and reveal the faithful. The command 'Seek and you will find' was given to the Jews before Christ was known, and once the rule of faith has been received, there is nothing further to seek. Heretics have no right to argue from Scripture because the Scriptures belong to the churches founded by the apostles, from which the true rule of faith has been handed down. The heretical teachings are later than, and derived from, the apostolic truth, and their teachers can be shown to be late innovators such as Marcion, Valentinus, and Apelles. Therefore heretics must be refused any debate over Scripture, since their doctrine, conduct, and origins already prove them false.

outline.move: Heresies were predicted and serve to test faith; the fall of prominent people does not prove heresy true; heresies come from philosophy and are condemned by the apostles.
The command 'Seek and you will find' was for the Jews before Christ was known; once the rule of faith is received, seeking has an end, and Christians should not seek among heretics.
The rule of faith is stated; heretics should not be admitted to disputes over Scripture because such contests are fruitless and the prior question is who owns the faith and the Scriptures.

The true doctrine is that handed down from Christ through the apostles to the apostolic churches; the apostles knew and taught the whole faith; heresies are later corruptions, as shown by their founders.
The parable of the wheat and tares shows heresies are later; heretics cannot prove apostolic origin; their doctrines were already condemned under the apostles; the true faith is prior and apostolic.
The apostolic churches, especially Rome, preserve the authentic tradition; Tertullian claims possession of the Scriptures; heretics are outsiders; their tampering with Scripture is exposed.
The disorderly conduct of heretics and their association with magicians and philosophers confirm their falsity; the treatise closes with a warning about the final judgment.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher in Carthage writing against heretics.

cast.name: Marcion
cast.who: A heretic from Pontus, a shipmaster and student of Stoicism, who taught a better god of tranquility and separated the New Testament from the Old.

cast.name: Valentinus
cast.who: A heretic who was a Platonist, who taught aeons, infinite forms, and a trinity of man.

cast.name: Apelles
cast.who: A deserter of Marcion's continence who fell into a relationship with a woman, then with Philumene; overcome by her spiritual activity, he wrote 'Phaneroseis' based on what he learned from her.

cast.name: Philumene
cast.who: A virgin (text uncertain) who had an angel of seduction; Apelles was induced by its signs and marvels to introduce a new heresy; later called a huge prostitute.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle, called the rock of the church and holder of the keys of the kingdom.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle to the nations, whose letters are cited against heretics.

cast.name: John
cast.who: The apostle beloved by the Lord, associated with the church of Smyrna through Polycarp.

cast.name: Clement
cast.who: Bishop of Rome, said to have been ordained by Peter (section 32).

cast.name: Polycarp
cast.who: Bishop of Smyrna, said to have been placed/established by John (section 32).

cast.name: Eleutherus
cast.who: Bishop of Rome under whom Marcion and Valentinus were expelled from the church.

cast.name: Hermogenes
cast.who: A heretic who taught that matter was uncreated and compared it to uncreated God, making it a goddess and mother of elements.

cast.name: Ebion
cast.who: The source refers to 'the heresy of Hebion', which defended circumcision and the law, without explicitly naming Hebion as a personal founder.

cast.name: Simon
cast.who: The Simonian school of magic, which serves angels and was condemned by Peter in the person of Simon himself.

cast.name: Nigidius
cast.who: A heretic named among those perverting the ways of the Lord.

voices.speaker: Heretics (quoted opponents)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by verbs of saying such as 'inquiunt' (sections 8, 22, 23), 'solent dicere' (section 22), and 'dicentes' implied; also 'inquiunt' in section 5.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted from Scripture)
voices.how_marked: Quoted as 'inquit' or from his letters; also cited by name with his letters referenced.

voices.speaker: Tertullian speaking in his own voice
voices.how_marked: Uses first-person possessives ('meo', 'mei') to claim apostolic inheritance in a direct address to heretics: 'Qui estis? quando, et unde venistis? quid in meo agitis, non mei?'

key_terms.sense: Factions or schools that choose their own doctrine in opposition to the apostolic faith
The fixed summary of Christian belief handed down from the apostles
A legal objection that bars an opponent from bringing a case; here, the argument that heretics have no right to use Scripture
The writings of the Old and New Testaments, which belong to the apostolic churches
The teaching handed down from Christ through the apostles to the churches
The twelve sent by Christ, whose teaching is the source of the true faith
Churches founded by the apostles, which preserve the authentic doctrine
The true Christian doctrine, identified with the apostolic tradition
The falsehood of heretical doctrine, opposed to the apostolic truth
The restless desire to seek beyond the received faith, which leads to heresy
Pagan secular learning, identified as the source of heretical doctrines
The ordered teaching and way of life of the church, opposed to heretical disorder
The body of teaching entrusted by Paul to Timothy, the fixed apostolic doctrine
The Holy Spirit, sent to lead the apostles into all truth

scripture: Tertullian uses the Septuagint/Vulgate book names and Psalm numbering. He refers to 'the first of Kingdoms' for 1 Samuel, 'Jesus son of Nave' for Joshua, and cites Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where they differ.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate (c. 200 AD), based on the mention of Eleutherus and the reign of Antoninus.
The identity of 'Hesidius Geta' and the precise title of his work are uncertain.
The exact reading of 'virgin(??) quadam Philumene' in section 6 is textually uncertain.
The identity of 'Nigidius' is uncertain.
The precise meaning of 'Gaiana haeresis' in section 33 is uncertain.
The source uses 'Hebion' in sections 33 and 34, while the standard modern form is 'Ebion'.
The source uses both 'Israël' (section 8) and 'Israel' (section 34).
The source uses 'Sadducaeorum' (genitive plural) in section 33, not 'Sadducaei' as nominative.
The source uses 'Corinthios' (accusative) in section 27, not 'Corinthii' as nominative.
The source uses 'Galatae' in section 27 as vocative/nominative plural.
The source uses 'Iacob' in section 8, the standard Latin form of Jacob.
The source uses 'Iudae' (genitive) in section 20 and 'Iudam' (accusative) in section 3, not 'Iudas' as nominative.
The source uses 'Matthia' (ablative) in section 20, not 'Matthias' as nominative.
The source uses 'Pontio Pilato' (ablative) in section 25, not 'Pontius Pilatus' as nominative.
The source uses 'Antonini' (genitive) in section 30, referring to the emperor's reign.
The source uses 'Mithra' (ablative or indeclinable) in section 39; standard form is 'Mithras'.
The source uses 'Vergilio' (ablative) in section 39, not 'Vergilius' as nominative.
The source uses 'Homeri' (genitive) in section 39, not 'Homerus' as nominative.
The source uses 'Aristotelem' (accusative) in section 7, not 'Aristoteles' as nominative.
The source uses 'Zenonis' (genitive) in section 7, not 'Zeno' as nominative.
The source uses 'Heracletus' (nominative) in section 7, a variant spelling of 'Heraclitus'.
The source uses 'Epicureis' (ablative/dative plural) in section 7, not 'Epicurei' as nominative.
The source uses 'Stoicis' (ablative/dative plural) in section 7, not 'Stoici' as nominative.
The source uses 'Platonicus' (adjective) in section 7, not 'Platonici' as nominative plural.
The source uses 'Timothee' (vocative) in section 25, not 'Timotheus' as nominative.
The source uses 'Tito' (dative/ablative) in section 6, not 'Titus' as nominative.
The source uses 'Moysen' (accusative) in section 8, not 'Moyses' as nominative.
The source uses 'Heliam' (accusative) in section 8, not 'Helias' as nominative.
The source uses 'Solomonis' (genitive) in section 7, not 'Solomon' as nominative.
The source uses 'Mariam' (accusative) in section 13, not 'Maria' as nominative.
The source uses various cases of 'Iesus Christus', 'Ioannes', 'Petrus', 'Paulus', and 'Eleutherus' throughout.
The source uses 'Hermogenes' (nominative) in section 34 and 'Hermogenis' (genitive) in section 33.
The source uses 'Simon' (nominative) and 'Simone' (ablative) in section 33.
